michael-denyer/pstack-claude

Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, Muse, OpenCode, Pi, and Prime Agent versions of Poteto's pstack. Rigorous agent workflows with Cursor primitives translated for other harnesses.

Language: JavaScript

README

# pstack

[![Buy Me A Coffee](https://img.shields.io/badge/Buy%20Me%20A%20Coffee-support-yellow?logo=buy-me-a-coffee&logoColor=white)](https://buymeacoffee.com/codenyer)
[![Mentioned in Awesome Claude Code](https://awesome.re/mentioned-badge.svg)](https://github.com/hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code)

Lauren Tan's [pstack](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack) is an opinionated Cursor skill stack that improves agent outcomes. This is a port for Claude Code, Codex, Pi, GitHub Copilot, Muse, and other agent harnesses. It tracks upstream and also carries named policy forks, each declared in [`tools/forks.json`](tools/forks.json).

Tell `poteto-mode` your goal and it will invoke the correct workflow for the task. It keeps your code concise, simple and verified.

For concurrency bugs and invariants that tests cannot reach, `/create-formal-verification-skill` picks the riskiest property in your code, verifies it with a tool that fits, and leaves a project skill the next agent reruns. The separate [agent-formal-verify](https://github.com/michael-denyer/agent-formal-verify) plugin goes deeper on the method, with guided TLA+ model checking, Lean proofs, and Kani for Rust.

## Built for Claude Code

This port translates upstream's Cursor skills for Claude Code before installation. [Upstream's Claude Code install](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/c742dd6/harness/pstack/claude-code) asks agents to translate Cursor names at runtime, using extra tokens and relying on them to apply the mapping correctly. This port also adds a SessionStart hook that routes tasks to `poteto-mode`.

## Install

<details>
<summary><strong>Claude Code</strong></summary>

Run in Claude Code 2.1.292 or later:

```text
/plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
/plugin install pstack@pstack-claude
```

Claude Code leaves auto-update off for third-party marketplaces, so pstack stays on the version you installed. To turn it on, run `/plugin`, open the **Marketplaces** tab, select `pstack-claude`, and choose **Enable auto-update**. To update once by hand, run `claude plugin update pstack@pstack-claude`.

</details>

<a id="codex"></a>
<details>
<summary><strong>Codex</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
codex plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
codex plugin add pstack@pstack-claude
```

Invoke a skill by typing `$` and its name, such as `$poteto-mode` or `$babysit`, then choosing its entry, which inserts `$pstack:<name>`. `/skills` lists every skill.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Pi</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
pi install git:github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
```

The package loads the skills and the pstack Pi extension, which adds the subagent, question, and wake-up tools the skills use, plus `/loop` and the routing instruction. Invoke a skill with `/skill:<name>`.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>GitHub Copilot</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
copilot plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
copilot plugin install pstack@pstack-claude
```

This installs pstack for the Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, which share `~/.copilot`. Start a new session afterwards. Copilot ships no default pstack models, so the first skill that needs one runs `setup-pstack` to pick from the models your account lists, and later sessions reuse that choice.

The Copilot build is tested on Copilot CLI 1.0.87 through 1.0.92. On those versions the routing hook's context reaches the session alongside other plugins' session-start context. If a later version keeps only one plugin's context, `setup-pstack` offers a [standing instruction](plugins/pstack/skills/setup-pstack/copilot.md#wire-it-in) for `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md` instead. On 1.0.92, once the CLI caches its computer-use experiment assignment, `copilot -p` sessions list no plugin skills and a `skill` call returns "Skill not found". Interactive sessions, the hooks, and the agents are unaffected.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Muse</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
muse plugins install ./plugins/pstack
muse plugins approve pstack
```

The first command installs the native Muse plugin bundle. The second approves its `SessionStart` hook and agent definitions, which Muse runs only after approval. Start a new session afterwards. Invoke a skill with `/<name>` (for example `/poteto-mode`), which Muse lists for each user-invocable skill.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Kimi Code CLI</strong></summary>

After a release containing `kimi.plugin.json` is published, close other Kimi sessions and install it in a fresh Kimi Code CLI session:

```text
/plugins install https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
/reload
```

To test an unreleased checkout, use `/plugins install /absolute/path/to/pstack-claude` instead, followed by `/reload`; Kimi copies the whole checkout, including Git metadata and local files, so use a clean, reviewed copy. To update, close other Kimi sessions, reinstall from the same source in a fresh session, and run `/reload`. Invoke a skill as `/skill:pstack:poteto-mode`; see the [Kimi mapping](plugins/pstack/skills/poteto-mode/references/kimi-tools.md) for tool guidance.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Grok Build</strong></summary>

```shell
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
grok plugin install "$PWD/plugins/pstack" --trust
grok plugin enable pstack
```

Start a new session and use `/poteto-mode` to load the skill explicitly. To update a local install, quit Grok sessions, inspect `grok plugin details pstack` and back up any edits in the installed copy, pull the checkout, run `grok plugin uninstall pstack --keep-data`, and repeat the last two commands. If pstack was disabled, disable it again before restarting. `grok plugin update` does not refresh a local install.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>MiniMax Code</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
mkdir -p "${MINIMAX_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.minimax}/plugins"
cp -R plugins/pstack "${MINIMAX_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.minimax}/plugins/pstack"
```

MiniMax Code loads each directory under `plugins/` in its data directory as a local plugin, and reads pstack through its Claude Code reader with the skills, agents, and routing hook. `mcode plugin list` shows it as `pstack@local`. To update after a `git pull`, delete the old `plugins/pstack` copy first, then run the `cp` line again; copying onto an existing copy nests it inside.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Antigravity (agy)</strong></summary>

Run in your terminal:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
agy plugin install ./plugins/pstack
```

This installs the native Antigravity plugin bundle (`skills`, `agents`, and `SessionStart` routing hook) into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/pstack`.

</details>

<a id="other-harnesses"></a>
<details>
<summary><strong>Other harnesses</strong></summary>

OpenCode (the CLI and the desktop app), Gemini CLI, Prime Agent, and skills-only Codex installs read skills from `~/.agents/skills/`. Run in your terminal:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills
for s in plugins/pstack/skills/*/; do
  target=~/.agents/skills/"$(basename "$s")"
  test -e "$target" || test -L "$target" || ln -s "$(pwd)/$s" "$target"
done
```

To update, run `git pull` in the clone, then run the `for` loop again to link skills added since the last run. These installs have no routing hook, so ask for `poteto-mode` by name or add a standing instruction to the harness's instruction file. See [shared installation](docs/reference.md#shared-skills-installation) for per-harness notes and uninstalling.

</details>

### Configure

pstack routes tasks to `poteto-mode` automatically. At session start, a hook injects an instruction that points the agent at it: the plugin's hook on Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Muse, and MiniMax Code, and the pstack extension on Pi. Codex runs the hook only after you trust it through `/hooks`, and Muse only after `muse plugins approve pstack`. Other harnesses have no hook.

Run `setup-pstack` to turn automatic routing on or off, change model defaults, or set a reasoning effort per role (`arena runners: opus @xhigh, fable @max`).

## Getting started

```text
Use poteto-mode to fix the search filter resetting when I change pages.
```

For a bug, it reproduces the failure, uses `how` and `why` to investigate, delegates the fix, then reruns the failing case. If the fix crosses a function boundary, it brings in `architect` before implementation. You receive the fix and the failing and passing evidence.

[Other playbooks](plugins/pstack/skills/poteto-mode/SKILL.md#playbooks) cover planning, features, refactoring, performance issues, investigations, prototypes, PR maintenance, shipping, and longer projects.

![poteto-mode on Claude Code, Codex, and Pi turns a request into verified work. Choose a playbook, plan and delegate with architect, arena, or swarm, then review and verify with interrogate, tests, and measurements. Project playbooks customize the workflow, and setup-pstack configures the model and reasoning effort per role. Supporting skills include how, why, and unslop.](assets/pstack-overview.png)

## Details

- [Skills and slash commands](docs/reference.md#slash-commands)
- [Runtime setup](docs/reference.md#runtime-support)
- [Models and dependencies](docs/reference.md#configuration-and-dependencies)
- [Maintenance and port scope](docs/reference.md#maintenance)

## Data handling

pstack has no server or telemetry. Anything its skills ask your agent to read, including session transcripts, goes to your model provider. Scripts run locally, and PR tools use your GitHub CLI login.

## Contributing

Thanks for helping make this port better. Bug reports, documentation fixes, and runtime improvements are welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the checks and where your change belongs. Report vulnerabilities privately as described in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

To support maintenance of this port, [buy the maintainer a coffee](https://buymeacoffee.com/codenyer).

# Marble Skill Taxonomy

An open, structured taxonomy of **what children learn** across the primary/elementary years — decomposed into fine-grained "micro-topics", wired into a prerequisite graph, and aligned to national curriculum standards. Produced by [Marble](https://withmarble.com).

> **Version:** `v1` · **Topics:** 1,861 · **Prerequisite edges:** 4,003 · **Subjects:** 9

## See it

![The taxonomy as a rotating 3D graph: every dot a micro-topic, colored by subject, wired by prerequisites](media/curriculum-viz.gif)

Every dot is a micro-topic, colored by subject; height is age; each thread is a prerequisite ([full-quality video](media/curriculum-viz.mp4)). Explore it interactively at [withmarble.com/curriculum](https://withmarble.com/curriculum) — tap any concept to trace everything a learner must master before it.


## What this is

Most curriculum data is either a flat list of standards or locked inside a product. This dataset is a **connected graph of learning**:

- **1,861 micro-topics** — a single, teachable idea (e.g. *"Building sentences"*, *"Apparent brightness of stars"*), each with a plain-language description, mastery **evidence** criteria, a type (conceptual / procedural / representational / language / meta), a subject + domain, and an approximate age range.
- **4,003 prerequisite dependencies** — a directed acyclic graph: *"topic X depends on prerequisite Y"*, each edge tagged `hard`/`soft` and carrying a one-line **reason**.
- **Curriculum alignment** — each micro-topic links to the standards it was distilled from (NGSS, Common Core, the UK National Curriculum, and more).
- **Teaching research** — 1,049 records. Coverage is partial; 812 topics have no research in this release.
- **Domain clusters** — 176 parent-friendly one-paragraph summaries per (subject, domain, age band).

### Subjects

| Subject | Topics |
|---|---:|
| Computing | 52 |
| English | 339 |
| Geography | 22 |
| History | 109 |
| Learning to Learn | 18 |
| Life Skills | 46 |
| Mathematics | 581 |
| Personal & Social Development | 118 |
| Science | 576 |

## Files

All data lives in [`data/`](data/) as UTF-8 JSON. See [`schema/`](schema/) for JSON Schemas and [`manifest.json`](data/manifest.json) for counts + SHA-256 checksums.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| [`data/topics.json`](data/topics.json) | The micro-topics (graph **nodes**). |
| [`data/dependencies.json`](data/dependencies.json) | Prerequisite **edges** (`topicId` depends on `prerequisiteId`). |
| [`data/curriculum-standards.json`](data/curriculum-standards.json) | The source curriculum standards, grouped by curriculum. |
| [`data/clusters.json`](data/clusters.json) | Parent-friendly domain summaries. |
| [`data/teaching-research.json`](data/teaching-research.json) | Teaching research joined by `topicId`, with explicit coverage and publication notes (~24 MB). |
| [`data/archived-teaching-research.json`](data/archived-teaching-research.json) | Historical guidance for merged or refocused topics, with original records and current topic associations. |
| [`data/manifest.json`](data/manifest.json) | Counts, per-subject breakdown, per-file checksums. |
| [`data/curriculum-alignments.json`](data/curriculum-alignments.json) | Scoped framework, jurisdiction and global age contexts; source for flat compatibility fields. |

The catalogue contains **17 sources / 7,743 expectations**. It includes 620 Australian Curriculum v9 content descriptions and 3,862 Ontario expectations from nine elementary documents. Ontario is exported as codes and official source links only; ingestion of source expectations is separate from authoring topic coverage. Ontario Grades 1–7 Mathematics have received focused taxonomy authoring passes. The [Grade 2 report](reports/ontario-grade2-mathematics-2026-10-23.md) distinguishes reused claims, extracted elementary claims and the concurrency gap; mappings do not certify learner mastery of every linked topic. The [Grade 3 report](reports/ontario-grade3-mathematics-2026-10-23.md) records reuse of 114 existing topics, the congruence extension and prerequisite repairs; no topics were added. The [Grade 4 report](reports/ontario-grade4-mathematics-2026-10-24.md) records reuse of 126 existing topics, two missing skills, two focused extractions and prerequisite repairs. The [Grade 5 report](reports/ontario-grade5-mathematics-2026-10-24.md) records reuse of 145 existing topics, one missing mathematical representation, one financial/civic concept and one focused extraction. The [Grade 6 report](reports/ontario-grade6-mathematics-2026-10-27.md) records reuse of 173 existing topics and five additions: two procedures, one focused extraction and two financial-content claims. The [Grade 7 report](reports/ontario-grade7-mathematics-2026-10-27.md) records reuse of 171 existing topics and two spatial additions; the square-root proposal was withdrawn.

Ontario Grade 5 Language adds 306 links across 161 existing topics, with no new topics. The [Grade 5 Language report](reports/ontario-grade5-language-2026-11-02.md) and [code-by-code mapping](reports/ontario-grade5-language-mapping-2026-11-02.json) record whole-topic reuse, prerequisite repairs, and the four remaining resource/performance conditions. Coverage links do not certify learner mastery.

Ontario Grade 6 Language adds 313 links across 168 topics, including three new claims and a suffix-evidence correction. The [Grade 6 Language report](reports/ontario-grade6-language-2026-11-02.md) and [code-by-code mapping](reports/ontario-grade6-language-mapping-2026-11-02.json) record 55 Full / 4 Partial specific expectations, with resource and performance conditions retained. This Language pass stops at primary Grade 6 (ages 11–12).

The Australian cleanup reviewed all 314 additions and 14 later edited IDs, consolidated repeated skills and redistributed bundled requirements. All 593 selected expectation codes remain linked. Those links do not certify whole-standard coverage: 572 previous Full claims have not been independently recertified. The 27 PE/movement descriptions remain excluded. Read the [cleanup report](reports/acara-v9-cleanup-2026-10-23.md) and [current area-by-area mapping counts](reports/acara-v9-scope-coverage.md).

See [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md) for sources and attribution.

### Adding curricula

The [public alignment contract](docs/curriculum-alignment-contract.md) now has a
[reviewed baseline](reports/scoped-alignment-baseline-2026-11-04.md) of 3,733 contexts.
Edit `data/curriculum-alignments.json` for associations and their ages; keep topic
claims in `data/topics.json`. The [version 2 scope model](docs/curriculum-alignment-contexts-v2.md)
preserves global guidance, international frameworks and separate jurisdiction age
intervals on one topic; version 1 remains supported by the codec.

Run `npm run alignments:generate`, `npm run validate`,
`npm run alignments:generated-check` and `npm test`, then submit the actual data
change in a normal PR. Generation refreshes flat topic standards/ages, the research
file's topic checksum binding and manifest checksums/counts. It uses only public
local files and preserves original timestamps; no private account is needed.
Authored research and its coverage must already be valid; this bounded command
does not author research or repair unrelated artifacts.

The [authoring and publication design](docs/taxonomy-authoring-and-publication.md)
describes downstream application deployment. This public baseline does not apply
changes to a live DB, migrate agent tools or activate the future publisher.

Curricula map onto one shared taxonomy. Keep subjects and domains consistent
across countries; a curriculum's learning-area labels do not create separate
subject trees.

- Reuse a topic when it assesses the same concept or operation. Add local
  examples without changing what mastery means.
- Review affected assessment guidance and learner estimates before changing a
  mastery claim. Assess independent procedures separately; topics do not track
  multiple difficulty levels.
- Record whole-expectation, component and prerequisite contributions explicitly.
  A topic–code link alone does not establish Full coverage.
- Reuse existing domains before adding a distinct new domain. Keep names
  consistent and avoid parallel country-specific domain trees.
- Keep each topic focused on a teachable concept or skill. A standard can link
  to several topics; its bundled requirements need not become one topic.
- Add country-specific topics where the knowledge genuinely differs, such as a
  country's history or constitutional arrangements. Use shared topics for common
  concepts and skills, with local examples where useful.

### A topic

```json
{
  "id": "mt_N8CpN1EJrP",
  "type": "CONCEPTUAL",
  "subject": "English",
  "domain": "Grammar & Punctuation",
  "name": "Building sentences",
  "description": "Understand that words combine to make sentences — a sentence expresses a complete thought…",
  "ageRangeStart": 4,
  "ageRangeEnd": 6,
  "centrality": 0.257,
  "evidence": [
    "Distinguish between complete sentences and fragments",
    "Compose a complete sentence with a subject and verb"
  ],
  "assessmentPrompt": "If {{name}} says something like \"The dog\", can they tell you that's not a complete sentence…?",
  "standards": ["ccss-ela:L.K.1f", "uk-nc-2013:Eng.App2.Y1.Sent.1"]
}
```

- `id` — stable identifier (`mt_…`), referenced by dependencies and by neighbours.
- `standards` — keys into `curriculum-standards.json` (`"<curriculum-slug>:<code>"`).
- `assessmentPrompt` — a natural-language check for the idea. Contains a `{{name}}` placeholder (the child's name); substitute or strip before display.

### A dependency

```json
{ "topicId": "mt__00ZSLnB7p", "prerequisiteId": "mt_VBl1T1sFCM", "strength": "hard",
  "reason": "Must understand vibrations make sound before finding volume patterns" }
```

`topicId` **depends on** `prerequisiteId`. Reverse the edge to get "unlocks".

## Teaching research

[`data/teaching-research.json`](data/teaching-research.json) adds **how a topic
might be taught** to the graph of what children learn. It contains **1,049 active topic records**. `coverage.missingTopicIds` and per-subject counts
make the **809 topics without research** explicit; absence is not a judgement
about whether a topic can be taught.

[`archived-teaching-research.json`](data/archived-teaching-research.json) preserves two historical records excluded from active coverage after a topic merge and a change in learning scope. Each entry includes the original topic and research record, its archive reason, and related current topic IDs. The archive also records the assessment prerequisite reference redirected after the merge.

The active `teaching-research.json` file has `schemaVersion: 1` and taxonomy `version: "v1"`. Each `records[]`
entry joins `topics.json` through `topicId` and contains:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pedagogy` | Original teaching summary, practices, representations and misconceptions. |
| `learn` | Portable learning guidance (`schemaVersion: 2`): a summary, activities, educational constraints and review notes. |
| `learn.activities[]` | Learner actions, intended insight, feedback, rationale and supporting source claims. No product artifact types or fit rankings. |
| `assess` | Original diagnostic/task, response levels, error patterns and next teaching moves; nullable in the public interface. |
| `sources` | Claim, named source, optional URL and the original author's verification flag. |
| `confidence` | Original authoring confidence; not an independent quality score. |
| `provenance` | Original authoring model and source record timestamps. The update timestamp also reflects the learning-guidance rewrite. |
| `publicationNotes` | Paths and curriculum codes for text omitted under the codes-only publication policy. |

`sourceClaims` exactly match `sources[].claim` after publication transformations.
A source may support a general principle or curriculum alignment; this does not
mean the proposed activity was tested. Some activities have no directly linked
source claim.

These records were agent-authored. The learning guidance was rewritten for
portability, checked by a separate factual critic, and sampled by a second agent.
Most original pedagogy and assessment were retained and may contain claims that
the updated guidance qualifies; chart-specific alignment repairs after #30 are
recorded in the affected learning-guidance review notes; read the constraints and review notes alongside
them. Sources were **not re-fetched or re-verified** for the initial publication;
later nutrition-guide checks are recorded in the affected review notes. Historical
`verified: true` and `confidence: "high"` are not new evidence ratings. Activities
are research-informed proposals, **not empirically validated interventions**.

Nutrition terminology corrections in [#63](https://github.com/withmarbleapp/os-taxonomy/pull/63)
update the existing Animal Nutrition, Balanced Diet & Food Groups, and Nutrients
in a Healthy Diet guidance, activities and assessment to distinguish nutrients
from food groups. Balanced-plate activities use food groups in a local guide;
the records retain their identities. See the
[review note](reports/acara-v9-design-technologies-authoring-review.md#teaching-guidance-correction-after-pr-review).

Some original research quoted restricted curriculum standards. Matched passages
are replaced with inline curriculum references, including inside citation claims;
all transformed paths are listed in `publicationNotes`. This is a conservative
mechanical omission pass, not comprehensive rights clearance. Consult the linked
upstream sources for their wording and terms. See [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md).

After the chart split in [#30](https://github.com/withmarbleapp/os-taxonomy/pull/30),
`mt_bESTSBB0wK` covers pie charts, `mt_H6LlpWgEYS` covers earlier line-graph
problem-solving, and `mt_HlNSurPVDp` has a separate construction-and-interpretation
record. The new record adapts existing graph research; it is not a fresh
literature review, and all reused source-verification flags are false. Its
assessment requires a complete constructed graph. The later grouped-charts
assessment routes graph-choice errors to data presentation and sector-angle
errors to pie charts.

The file is bound to the exact `topics.json` bytes through `topicFileSha256`.
Regenerate the research projection when the canonical topic file changes, even
when topic IDs remain stable.

## Using it

Pure data — no runtime, no dependencies. Load the JSON and go.

```js
import topics from './data/topics.json' with { type: 'json' };
import deps from './data/dependencies.json' with { type: 'json' };

const byId = new Map(topics.topics.map(t => [t.id, t]));
const prereqs = deps.dependencies
  .filter(d => d.topicId === 'mt_N8CpN1EJrP')
  .map(d => byId.get(d.prerequisiteId).name);
```

Join teaching guidance to a topic:

```js
import research from './data/teaching-research.json' with { type: 'json' };

const guidanceByTopic = new Map(research.records.map(r => [r.topicId, r]));
const guidance = guidanceByTopic.get('mt_N8CpN1EJrP'); // undefined: English is not covered yet
const activities = guidance?.learn.activities ?? [];
```

Validate structure, research coverage, evidence links and checksums:

```bash
node scripts/validate.mjs
node --test scripts/teaching-research.test.mjs
```

## Marble Builder

The [`marble-builder` agent skill](.agents/skills/marble-builder/SKILL.md)
helps turn a child's age and a user-confirmed goal into a standalone HTML
learning experience that works offline by default. It uses topic prerequisites
and available teaching research,
develops a targeted research brief when needed, and agrees a concept with you
before building. Experiences use visual interactions, scaffolding, UI-assessed
transfer tasks and optional extensions. Spatial topics use Three.js with direct
scene manipulation and a crafted cel-shaded look with flat colors and black
outlines. Visual simulations must meet a beauty, craft and polish bar as well as
work correctly. The public skill includes Marble-derived UI tokens, tactile
controls refined in Moon Visit and Sky Colour Explorer, and the openly licensed
Baloo 2 font, with one title and one instruction
visible at a time: a small top-left title and a large, prominent instruction or
explanation, plus concise button labels paired with icons. [Water Lab](https://withmarble.com/water-lab) is the visual quality
reference. The agent renders, inspects and iterates
in the browser rather than stopping at the first working HTML file.

The skill includes [five runnable examples with readable source, key-state
screenshots and design notes](.agents/skills/marble-builder/references/examples.md):
Moon Visit, Sky Colour Explorer, Hidden Cubes, Bee Builder and Otter Forest. The notes explain
what to borrow and where each prototype has limits or exceptions.

Optional connected LLM mode requires explicit author approval and a learning goal
whose open-ended reasoning or text production cannot be adequately supported
locally. That mode requires internet and a separate account connection; ChatGPT
plan usage is a preview option for eligible local/open-source integrations.

In Codex, open this repository and invoke `$marble-builder`, for example:

> Use $marble-builder to help my 8-year-old understand why equivalent
> fractions represent the same quantity.

Other agents can follow the linked `SKILL.md` directly. No Marble account or
hosting is required. New reusable teaching research can optionally be proposed
as a separate PR, with no child-specific information included.

## Install ECC

> [!IMPORTANT]
> ECC 2.2 includes guided package setup for Claude Code, Codex, and Kimi Code.
> The universal package requires Node.js 18 or newer. Claude plugin setup also
> requires Git and Claude Code 2.1 or newer on `PATH`.

### Recommended: universal guided setup

For Claude Code plugin setup, updates, scope changes, and hook-profile changes:

```bash
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup
```

#### Windows first-time walkthrough

If you are new to command-line tools, use this copy-and-paste path:

1. Install Node.js 18 or newer, Git, and Claude Code.
2. Open **PowerShell** from the Windows Start menu.
3. Confirm that each prerequisite is available:

   ```powershell
   node --version
   git --version
   claude --version
   ```

4. Run the guided installer:

   ```powershell
   npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup
   ```

5. For a typical personal setup, choose **Global user**, choose **Standard** hooks, and confirm.
6. Start a new Claude Code session and run `/plugin list` to verify that `ecc@ecc` is enabled.

This path does not require cloning the repository. If any prerequisite command is not found, install or repair that prerequisite before rerunning ECC setup.

If npm reports a version or cache error, confirm the registry version before retrying:

```bash
npm view ecc-universal version
```

ECC 2.2 supports the same guided setup through modern package runners:

| Package runner | Guided setup command |
|---|---|
| npm / npx | `npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup` |
| pnpm | `pnpm dlx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup` |
| Yarn 2+ | `yarn dlx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup` |
| Bun | `bunx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup` |

The examples select [the published ECC 2.2.3 release](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ecc-universal/v/2.2.3), matching this repository's release version. A version pin is not a security audit or an integrity check. Review the release source and registry integrity before running package code; use a reviewed checkout for unreleased changes.

Yarn Classic 1 does not provide `yarn dlx`; use `npx`, install the package globally, or upgrade Yarn for a temporary one-shot run.

The wizard inventories the official marketplace and every native Claude install scope before making changes, then installs, updates, or safely moves `ecc@ecc` to the scope you choose. Rerun the same command whenever you want to update ECC, change scope, or change its hook profile. This setup wizard currently configures the Claude Code plugin; use the multi-harness wizard below for Codex or Kimi Code.

To configure more than one coding agent in one reviewed flow, use the multi-harness wizard:

```bash
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 install --guided
```

It lets you select any combination of Claude Code, Codex, and Kimi Code, shows each install channel and destination, preflights every selection before the first write, and asks for one final confirmation.

| Harness | Guided install behavior |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | Native `ecc@ecc` plugin with one `user`, `project`, or `local` scope and an ECC hook profile |
| Codex | Native Codex marketplace/plugin lifecycle; hook review and trust remain Codex-owned |
| Kimi Code | Managed project files under `./.kimi-code`; ECC hooks, model/provider settings, and authentication are not configured |

For automation, make every provider-specific choice explicit:

```bash
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 install --guided \
  --harness claude --harness codex --harness kimi \
  --claude-scope local --claude-hooks standard \
  --profile core --yes
```

Verify the native guided Codex path and managed Kimi path without writing first:

```bash
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 install --guided --harness codex --dry-run
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 install --profile core --target kimi --dry-run
```

Additional package-name commands are also available through the 2.2 alias:

```bash
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 consult "security reviews" --target claude
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 install --profile minimal --target claude --with capability:machine-learning
npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 doctor --target kimi
```

Do not use `npx ecc-install --profile minimal --target claude`: `ecc-install` is a binary name inside `ecc-universal`, not a separately published npm package.

ECC also ships advanced managed adapters for `cursor`, `antigravity`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `codebuddy`, `joycode`, `qwen`, `zed`, `hermes`, and `openclaw`. Those targets still use their documented `ecc install --target ...` paths until each adapter has passed the guided collision, update, repair, and uninstall lifecycle matrix. Neither wizard silently installs into every detected harness.

### Pick one path only (per harness)

You can use ECC with Claude Code, Codex, and other harnesses at the same time. Choose one install method for each harness:

- **Recommended default:** run the guided Claude plugin setup above
- **Also supported for Claude Code:** use the [native plugin commands](#claude-code-details)
- **Available in release 2.2:** guided package setup for Claude Code, Codex, and Kimi Code
- **Works:** Claude Code plugin + Codex native plugin
- **Works:** Claude Code plugin + the legacy Codex sync flow
- **Avoid:** Claude Code plugin + full Claude manual install
- **Avoid:** Codex sync + Codex marketplace plugin

**Do not stack install methods.** Installing ECC twice into the same harness can duplicate skills, commands, hooks, or configuration; installing it once into multiple harnesses does not.

If you already layered multiple installs and things look duplicated, skip straight to [Reset / Uninstall ECC](#reset--uninstall-ecc).

**Install trouble?** Open the short [install or runtime problem form](https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC/issues/new?template=install-problem.yml), or run `ecc feedback`. ECC never uploads diagnostics automatically.

### Claude Code details

Alternatively, run Claude Code's native plugin commands inside Claude Code:

```text
/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC
/plugin install ecc@ecc
```

The native path installs ECC's skills, agents, commands, and plugin-managed hooks. If you choose it, stop there. Do not also run a full manual install into Claude Code.

Claude Code owns these built-in commands, including their errors when a marketplace, plugin, or conflicting scope already exists. ECC cannot intercept that parser. If either native command reports an existing install or scope conflict, use the 2.2 guided setup or resolve the conflicting Claude plugin scope before retrying; do not layer a manual install on top.

After ECC is installed, `/ecc:configure-ecc` is the namespaced in-Claude reconfiguration skill. It delegates to the same safe setup flow, but it is available only after the plugin is installed and cannot replace Claude Code's built-in `/plugin` command during a first install.

Claude Code plugins cannot distribute `rules`, so add only the rule packs you actually want:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC.git
cd ECC
mkdir -p ~/.claude/rules/ecc
cp -R rules/common ~/.claude/rules/ecc/
cp -R rules/typescript ~/.claude/rules/ecc/  # replace with your stack
```

Start with `rules/common` plus one language or framework pack you actually use. If you install the plugin, do not run `./install.sh --profile full` afterward.

<details>
<summary><strong>Prefer settings.json? Add the marketplace declaratively</strong></summary>

Add directly to your `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "ecc": {
      "source": {
        "source": "github",
        "repo": "affaan-m/ECC"
      }
    }
  },
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "ecc@ecc": true
  }
}
```

This gives you the same result as the two `/plugin` commands above.
</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Naming + migration note (ecc@ecc, affaan-m/ECC, ecc-universal)</strong></summary>

ECC has three public identifiers, and they are not interchangeable:

- GitHub source repo: `affaan-m/ECC`
- Claude marketplace/plugin identifier: `ecc@ecc`
- npm package: `ecc-universal`

This is intentional. Anthropic marketplace/plugin installs are keyed by a canonical plugin identifier, so ECC uses `ecc@ecc` to keep tool names and slash-command namespaces short enough for strict Desktop/API validators. Older posts may still show the former long marketplace identifier; treat that as a legacy alias only. Separately, the npm package stayed on `ecc-universal`, so npm installs and marketplace installs intentionally use different names.

npm releases are cut per version tag, not per commit, so `ecc-universal` tracks releases (2.1, 2.2, ...) rather than every push to `main`. Install from git if you want the bleeding edge.

If your local Claude setup was wiped or reset, that does not mean you need to repurchase anything. Start with `node scripts/ecc.js list-installed`, then run `node scripts/ecc.js doctor` and `node scripts/ecc.js repair` before reinstalling. That usually restores ECC-managed files without rebuilding your setup.
</details>

jgraph/drawio-desktop

Official electron build of draw.io

Language: JavaScript

Stars: 63,816

Forks: 5,809

README

About
----- 

**drawio-desktop** is a diagramming desktop app based on [Electron](https://electronjs.org/) that wraps the [core draw.io editor](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio).

Download built binaries from the [releases section](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-desktop/releases).

**Can I use this app for free?** Yes, under the GPL v3 license. If you don't change the code and accept it is provided "as-is", you can use it for any purpose.

Windows installation
--------------------

Three flavours of Windows download are published on the [releases page](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-desktop/releases):

- `draw.io-<version>-windows-installer.exe` — NSIS installer. Installs **per-machine** into `Program Files` and **requires administrator privileges**.
- `draw.io-<version>.msi` — MSI installer. Installs **per-user** into the user's profile and **does not require administrator privileges**. Use this one if you don't have admin rights on your machine.
- `draw.io-<version>-windows.zip` — portable build. Extract the zip anywhere and run `draw.io.exe`, with no installation (and therefore without admin rights). File-type associations are not registered.

The Microsoft Store (APPX) build is also installable per-user without admin rights via the Store.

### Windows on Arm

draw.io Desktop is built natively for Windows on Arm (ARM64) and is supported on Windows 11 ARM64 devices. Two native ARM64 downloads are published with every release:

- `draw.io-arm64-<version>-windows-arm64-installer.exe` — NSIS installer, per-machine, requires administrator privileges.
- `draw.io-arm64-<version>-windows-arm64-no-installer.exe` — portable build, no installation or admin rights needed.

The MSI and Microsoft Store builds are x64 only and run under emulation on ARM64 devices. ARM64 builds up to and including 31.4.4 were shipped with auto-update disabled; install a newer release manually once, after which the ARM64 installer build updates itself like x64.

Linux installation
------------------

If you manage AppImages with [AppImageLauncher](https://github.com/TheAssassin/AppImageLauncher), you need a 3.0 release of it (currently labelled beta). Since 31.4.2 the AppImage uses the static AppImage runtime so that it no longer depends on the end-of-life `libfuse2`, and AppImageLauncher 2.2.0, the last stable release, cannot load a static runtime. The app then fails to start with:

```
fuse: memory allocation failed
squashfuse 0.5.2 (c) 2012 Dave Vasilevsky
...
Can't open squashfs image: Bad address
```

Install a current AppImageLauncher from its [releases page](https://github.com/TheAssassin/AppImageLauncher/releases), which provides .deb packages, or uninstall AppImageLauncher altogether. It is not needed to run the AppImage. See [#2538](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-desktop/issues/2538) for the detail.

Updates
-------

How draw.io Desktop updates depends on how it was installed:

- **Windows installer (`.exe`), macOS and AppImage:** new versions download in the background. When one is ready, the editor shows a notice, and clicking it or Help > Restart to Update installs it straight away. Otherwise it is installed when you quit draw.io. The Windows installer is per-machine, so the update asks for administrator rights.
- **MSI, Windows zip, Windows ARM64 portable, deb and rpm:** draw.io tells you when a new version is available and links to its release page. Install it the same way as the current one.
- **Microsoft Store, Snap and Flatpak:** the store updates the app, and draw.io does not check for updates.

Extras > Automatic Updates (draw.io > Check for Updates Automatically on macOS) turns the background checks off. Help > Check for Updates still works. For centrally managed installs, set the `DRAWIO_DISABLE_UPDATE=true` environment variable or pass `--disable-update` to turn off all update checks, or set `DRAWIO_NO_SILENT_UPDATE=true` or pass `--no-silent-update` so that draw.io asks before it downloads an update.

Security
--------

draw.io Desktop is designed to be completely isolated from the Internet, apart from the update process. This checks github.com once a day for a newer version and downloads it from an AWS S3 bucket owned by Github. To disable the update check entirely (e.g. for centrally-managed installs), set the `DRAWIO_DISABLE_UPDATE=true` environment variable or pass `--disable-update` on launch. All JavaScript files are self-contained, the Content Security Policy forbids running remotely loaded JavaScript.

No diagram data is ever sent externally, nor do we send any analytics about app usage externally. The Content Security Policy on the web part of the interface forbids remotely-loaded JavaScript and restricts the application's own network connections to itself, so the app cannot transmit your diagrams or otherwise phone home. Note that a diagram can reference external media - for example an image, background or font loaded from a URL embedded in the diagram - and these are fetched when the diagram is opened so that it renders correctly. Opening a diagram from an untrusted source may therefore trigger a request to the referenced URL, which can reveal metadata such as your IP address to that server; no diagram content is transmitted.

Security and isolating the app are the primarily objectives of draw.io desktop. If you ask for anything that involves external connections enabled in the app by default, the answer will be no.

Support
-------

Support is provided on a reasonable business constraints basis, but without anything contractually binding. All support is provided via this repo. There is no private ticketing support for non-paying users.

Purchasing draw.io for Confluence or Jira does not entitle you to commercial support for draw.io desktop.

Developing
----------

**draw.io** is a git submodule of **drawio-desktop**. To get both you need to clone recursively:

`git clone --recursive https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-desktop.git`

To run this:
1. `npm install` (in the root directory of this repo)
2. [internal use only] export DRAWIO_ENV=dev if you want to develop/debug in dev mode.
3. `npm start` _in the root directory of this repo_ runs the app. For debugging, use `npm start --enable-logging`.

Note: If a symlink is used to refer to drawio repo (instead of the submodule), then symlink the `node_modules` directory inside `drawio/src/main/webapp` also.

To fork the project, make your own changes and build an (unsigned) app for personal use, see [doc/BUILDING_FOR_PERSONAL_USE.md](doc/BUILDING_FOR_PERSONAL_USE.md).

The release process (GitHub Actions builds, signing and publishing) is described in [doc/RELEASE_PROCESS.md](doc/RELEASE_PROCESS.md).

Local Storage and Session Storage is stored in the AppData folder:

- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/draw.io`
- Windows: `C:\Users\<USER-NAME>\AppData\Roaming\draw.io\`

Not open-contribution
---------------------

draw.io is closed to contributions (unless a maintainer permits it, which is extremely rare).

The level of complexity of this project means that even simple changes 
can break a _lot_ of other moving parts. The amount of testing required 
is far more than it first seems. If we were to receive a PR, we'd have 
to basically throw it away and write it how we want it to be implemented.

We are grateful for community involvement, bug reports, & feature requests. We do
not wish to come off as anything but welcoming, however, we've
made the decision to keep this project closed to contributions for 
the long term viability of the project.
